title: Goldman Sachs – inside the elite investment bank (Klausur 2026)
text: Goldman Sachs was founded in New York in 1869 by Marcus Goldman, a German immigrant who traded commercial paper; his son-in-law Samuel Sachs joined in 1882. For 130 years the firm was a private partnership: the partners owned the bank, shared its profits and were personally liable for its losses. It became one of the leading investment banks in the world and only went public in 1999. The partner title has survived the IPO: every two years a small group of managing directors is elected partner, the most coveted step of a Goldman career.

Today the group employs around 45,000 people in more than 40 countries, from its headquarters at 200 West Street in Manhattan – a discreet tower with hardly any visible signage. Activities are organised in large business divisions, each with its own results: Global Banking & Markets (mergers and acquisitions advice, underwriting, trading for clients) and Asset & Wealth Management. Inside them, small deal teams and trading desks work for clients under heavy time pressure. The career ladder is short and well known: analyst, associate, vice president, managing director, partner. Powerful control divisions – Compliance, Risk, Legal, Controllers – set limits, procedures and reporting obligations; since 2008 Goldman is a bank holding company supervised by the Federal Reserve. Thousands of engineers and operations staff build and run the trading platforms and process transactions. The CEO, David Solomon (since 2018), leads with a management committee and is accountable to the board.

Recruitment is extremely selective: each year hundreds of thousands of students apply for a few thousand internship and analyst places, mostly from elite universities. New analysts are trained intensively and then learn on the job from associates and vice presidents. In 1979 co-chairman John Whitehead wrote down the firm's business principles, still published today: “Our clients' interests always come first”, “Our assets are our people, capital and reputation”, “We stress teamwork in everything we do”. The firm's values are partnership, client service, integrity and excellence. Former senior partner Gus Levy summed up the attitude as being “greedy, but long-term greedy”. So many alumni have joined governments and central banks – Robert Rubin, Henry Paulson, Mario Draghi among others – that critics speak of “Government Sachs”.

Pay is high and largely variable. Compensation and benefits absorb roughly a third of the firm's revenues; bonuses are fixed once a year according to individual and team results, and a growing part of senior pay is deferred in shares that can be clawed back in case of misconduct. Employees are evaluated every year through 360-degree reviews and ranked against their peers; the lowest performers are regularly asked to leave.

The culture is also criticised. In 2010 Goldman paid 550 million dollars to settle a US lawsuit claiming that it had misled clients on a mortgage product it had helped design. In 2012 executive director Greg Smith resigned with an op-ed in the New York Times describing the culture as “toxic and destructive” and claiming that some managers called their own clients “muppets”. In 2020 the firm paid more than 2.9 billion dollars to settle the 1MDB scandal, in which one of its partners had helped divert billions from a Malaysian state fund. In 2021 a group of first-year analysts circulated an internal survey: they reported working close to 100 hours a week, sleeping about five hours a night and suffering from their working conditions. Management answered by raising junior salaries and by reaffirming a rule protecting Saturdays from work. In 2019 the bank relaxed its strict suit-and-tie dress code; David Solomon himself performs as a DJ at festivals.
